documentNotes.title: Please read this first:
documentNotes.statement:
1. The time available for the theoretical competition is 4 hours. There are three questions.
2. Use only the pen provided.
3. You are provided with ***Writing sheet*** and additional paper. You can use the additional paper for drafts of your solutions but these papers will not be checked. Your final solutions which will be evaluated should be on the ***Writing sheets***. Please use as little text as possible. You should mostly use equations, numbers, figures and plots.
4. Use only the front side of ***Writing sheets.*** Write only inside the bordered area.
5. Begin each question on a separate sheet.
6. Fill the boxes at the top of each sheet of paper with your country (**Country),** your student code (**Student Code**), the question number (**Question Number)**, the progressive number of each sheet **(Page Number**), and the total number of ***Writing sheets*** used (**Total Number of Pages**). If you use some blank ***Writing sheets*** for notes that you do not wish to be evaluated, put a large X across the entire sheet and do not include it in your numbering.
7. At the end of the exam, arrange all sheets for each problem in the following order:
   - Used ***Writing sheets*** in order;
   - The sheets you do not wish to be evaluated
   - Unused sheets and the printed question.

   Place the papers inside the envelope and leave everything on your desk. You are not allowed to take any paper out of the room.

transcription.notes: Word export: the text layer keeps the prose but loses Greek letters and most formulas, so it was used only as a spelling cross-check. Point values are printed only per part (Question 1: 10, Question 2: 8, Question 3: 12; 30 in total), so problem points and totalPoints are null. Kept verbatim as printed: the Cyrillic „и“ in Question 1, part 5 a) („Calculate φ0, ψ и θ“); „k1=μ, k2 = ∞“ written without subscripts; „[2 point]“, „[0.5 point]“ and „[1point]“ in the solutions; „decelerates afterwards..“ (double period); „Kirchgoff“ (a name); „reflects form the mirror“ (a real word, not a non-word misspelling); „the same(here f“; „a superconducting electromagnets“; degrees printed as a superscript 0 (90⁰). Scientific content kept verbatim and noted: in the solution to Question 3 c) the formulas E_n = m_He/(m_He + m_n) and E_He = m_n/(m_He + m_n) omit the factor E0; in 3 g) the unit of B is printed „Ts“ (tesla). Question 1 part 5 opens with the printed data block „Numerical data:“, placed at the start of part 5 a). The solutions file matches the paper (same competition, same three questions); the solutions for Question 1 parts 3 and 4 carry no printed points at the numbered heading, only at the sub-items.

problems.title: A block with an object
problems.statement:
A weightless rod is attached to a massive block with a mass M. An object with a mass m is attached to the rod by a weightless string of length R. The object can rotate in a vertical plane not touching the rod. The coefficient of friction between the block and the floor depends on the direction of sliding, $k1=\mu$, $k2 = \infty$. The object is launched with an initial velocity $V_0$ in the direction as shown in the picture 1. $V_0$ is sufficiently big so that the object makes at least one rotation around the rod.

In this problem you are asked to examine the movement of the system during the first rotation of the object. You can assume that the block does not detach from the floor and does not turn over and that the string is stretched while the object is moving. Let’s describe the position of the object by the angle $\varphi$ (Fig 1). Assume $M \gg m$.

figures.caption: Fig.1
figures.alt: A block M on a hatched floor with a vertical rod; a point mass m on a string of length R hangs from the rod top and moves on a dashed circle; the angle φ is measured from the rod; at the lowest point the initial velocity V0 points left; below the floor, arrows k1 (left) and k2 (right).

parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** In this part of the question assume that the parameters are such that the block does not move at all. Derive the condition that will guarantee that the change in absolute velocity of the object is considerably smaller than $V_0$ in the process of rotation.
parts.statementAfter: From this point onwards you can assume that the block’s velocity is considerably smaller than $V_0$, and that the change in absolute velocity of the object during first rotation is considerably smaller than $V_0$.

parts.statement: **[*2 points*]** Find the minimum initial velocity $V_0^{\min}$ which will cause the block to slide when the object is rotating.

parts.label: 3. a)
parts.statement:
For $V_0 > V_0^{\min}$ find:

**[*1 point*]** At which angle $\varphi_0$ sliding will start;

parts.label: 3. b)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** At which angle $\psi$ the velocity of block’s motion *V* will be largest.

parts.label: 4. a)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** Find $V_{max}$ which corresponds to the angle $\psi$ from b) above;

parts.label: 4. b)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** Write down the condition for angle $\theta$, at which the block stops.

parts.label: 5. a)
parts.statement:
Numerical data:

$$\mu = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1 \approx 0.57,$$

$$g = 10\ m/s^2,$$

$$M = 10\ kg$$

$$V_0 = 10\ m/s,$$

$$R = 0.1\ m,$$

$$m = 0.057\ kg.$$

**[0.5 *points*]** Calculate $\varphi_0$, $\psi$ и $\theta$.

parts.label: 5. c)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** For the given numerical values, calculate the displacement of the block in one rotation of the object.

parts.label: 5. d)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** In first non vanishing order, estimate the change in the velocity of the object at the lowest point after the first rotation in comparison to $V_0$.

answer.note: Relative change ΔV/V0; the solution estimates −5*10^-4 by order of magnitude and gives the exact value −3*10^-4.

problems.statementAfterParts:
***Note:***

The following formulas might be useful for solution:

$$\cos\varphi + \mu\ \sin\varphi = \sqrt{1+\mu^2}\ \cos(\varphi - \alpha),$$

$$\cos\varphi - \mu\ \sin\varphi = \sqrt{1+\mu^2}\ \cos(\varphi + \alpha),$$

where $\alpha = \operatorname{arctg}\mu = \arccos(1/\sqrt{1+\mu^2}) = \arcsin(\mu/\sqrt{1+\mu^2})$.

$$\int\cos\varphi d\varphi = \sin\varphi,\ \int\sin\varphi d\varphi = -\cos\varphi$$

solution.statement:
1. **[*1 point*]** From the energy conservation law for the object:

$$V_0^{\,2} - V_{top}^{\,2} = 4gR \approx 2V_0\Delta V,\quad \Delta V / V = 2gR/V_0^{\,2} \ll 1$$

2. **[2 *point*]** Maximal angle of deviation of the floor’s total reaction force (Normal force + friction force) from vertical is

$$\alpha = \operatorname{arctg}\mu.$$

Denote

$$T = mV_0^{\,2}/R,\qquad \omega = V_0/R.$$

From the picture above we can see (see Fig.2) that the maximum angle of deviation of

$$M\vec{g} + \vec{T}$$

is $\arcsin(T/Mg)$ when $T \le Mg$ ($M\vec{g} + \vec{T}$ is tangent to the circle). If the deviation angle of $M\vec{g} + \vec{T}$ from the vertical line is greater than $\alpha$, then the equilibrium is impossible and the block will start to slide. The condition that we are looking for is

$$V_0^{\min} = \sqrt{\frac{MgR\mu}{m\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}}$$

3. From Fig 2, the beginning of sliding corresponds to point B. The block accelerates on the portion of path *BC, and decelerates afterwards.*. Since the line intersects the rotation circle at two points, $\angle ABO < \pi/2$, and therefore from the sine theorem for the triangle *ABO* :

$$\angle ABO = \arcsin\left(\mathrm{Mg}\frac{\sin\alpha}{m\omega^2\ R}\right) = \arcsin\left(\frac{\mu Mg}{m\omega^2\ R\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right)$$

a) **[*1 point*]** Then

$$\varphi_0 = \alpha + \angle ABO = \operatorname{arctg}\mu + \arcsin\left(\frac{\mu Mg}{m\omega^2\ R\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right).$$

b) **[*1 point*]** Similarly

$$\psi = \alpha + \pi - \angle ABO = \operatorname{arctg}\mu + \pi - \arcsin\left(\frac{\mu Mg}{m\omega^2\ R\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right).$$

4. To calculate the acceleration we can first decompose the forces into x and y components and write down Newton’s second law

$$F_{\mathrm{friction}} = \mu\ \mathrm{N} = \mu\,(M\mathrm{g} + T\cos\varphi)$$

$$M\,\mathrm{a}(\varphi) = T\sin\varphi - F_{\mathrm{friction}} = T\sin\varphi - \mu\,(M\mathrm{g} + T\cos\varphi)$$

Then

$$V(\varphi) = \int a(\varphi)dt = \int\frac{a(\varphi)d\varphi}{\omega}$$

Integration gives us:

$$V(\varphi) = -\left(\frac{T}{\omega M}(\cos\varphi + \mu\sin\varphi) + \frac{\mu g\varphi}{\omega}\right) + \left(\frac{T}{\omega M}(\cos\varphi_0 + \mu\sin\varphi_0) + \frac{\mu g\varphi_0}{\omega}\right).$$

a) **[*1point*]** Then

$$V_{\mathrm{max}} = \mathrm{v}(\psi) = 2\frac{T}{\omega M}\sqrt{1+\mu^2-\mu^2\left(\frac{Mg}{T}\right)^2}\ -\ \frac{\mu g}{\omega}\left(\pi - 2\arcsin\ \frac{\mu Mg}{T\sqrt{1+\mu^2}}\right)$$

b) **[*1 point*]** The condition for $\theta$ : $V(\theta) = 0$

$$\frac{T}{\omega M}(\cos\varphi_0 + \mu\sin\varphi_0) + \frac{\mu g\varphi_0}{\omega} = \frac{T}{\omega M}(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta) + \frac{\mu g\theta}{\omega}$$

5. The values are such that $\dfrac{Mg}{T} = \dfrac{1}{\mu} = 1/(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - 1)$.

a) **[0.5 *point*]** Using this equality we get :

$$\varphi_0 = 90^{0},\ \psi = 90^{0} + 2\operatorname{arctg}(0.57) \approx 150^{0},\ \theta = 180^{0}$$

b) **[0.5 *point*]**

$$V_{\mathrm{max}} = 2\frac{\mu g}{\omega}(\mu - \operatorname{arctg}\mu) \approx 6*10^{-3}\mathrm{m/s} \ll V_0$$

c) **[*1 point*]** Displacement is

$$\mathrm{S} = \int\frac{V(\varphi)d\varphi}{\omega}.$$

Plug in

$$\mu = \frac{\pi}{2} - 1,\ \varphi_0 = \frac{\pi}{2},\ \theta = \pi,$$

We get

$$\mathrm{S} = \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - 1\right)\left(2 + \frac{\pi^2}{8} - \pi\right)\mathrm{g}/\omega^2 \approx 5.3*10^{-5}\mathrm{m}.$$

d) **[*1 point*]** The change in object’s velocity occurs because the kinetic energy is lowered due to work by friction force. In first nonvanishing order, the change in velocity is determined from the Law of change in energy, where the work of friction force is calculated assuming constant absolute velocity of the object:

$$mV_0\Delta V = \int F_{friction}ds = -\int_{\varphi_0}^{\theta}\mu(\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{T}\cos\varphi)\,\mathrm{v}(\varphi)\frac{d\varphi}{\omega}.$$

By order of magnitude

$$\frac{\Delta V}{V_0} \propto -\frac{\mu MgS}{mV_0^{\,2}} \propto -5*10^{-4}.$$

The exact value: $-3*10^{-4}$

problems.statement: This problem consists of two unrelated parts

parts.label: A.
parts.statement: **[5 points]**Find the current through resistance *R = 17 Ohm*, in the Fig 2. The internal resistance of the battery is *r = 3 Ohm*, Electromotive force *ε = 10 V*. The section with resistance *R*₁= *1 Ohm* and *R*₂= *6 Ohm* is repeated 17 times

figures.caption: Fig.2
figures.alt: Ladder circuit: a source ε, r on the left; along the top wire a chain of resistors R1, R1, … R1 (dashed break indicating repetition); between the top and bottom wires shunt resistors R2 after the source and after each R1, and the load R at the far right end.

parts.label: B.
parts.statement: **[3 Points]** A thin lens creates the image of an object. If a flat mirror is put right next to this lens perpendicular to the main optical axis, then this whole system creates an image with the same absolute optical magnification as before provided that the object is at the same distance as before. Determine the magnification.

solution.statement:
**A**

**[5 points]** Direct calculation of the current through resistance R is very complicated and takes a long time.

Therefore let’s first examine the Fig 4. Let current *I flow through* resistance *R*ₓ. Then the current through resistance *R*₂ will be

$$I_2 = \frac{R_x + R_1}{R_2}I$$

Accordingly the current through the source is

$$I_B = \frac{R_x + (R_1 + R_2)}{R_2}I$$

The second rule of Kirchgoff for external contour is

$$\frac{R_x + (R_1 + R_2)}{R_2}I\cdot r + I\cdot(R_1 + R_x) = \varepsilon$$

From here we can find the value of current *I*, plugging in the values *R*₁ and *R*₂. Then

$$I = \frac{(2/3)\varepsilon}{(R_x + 3)}$$

If we take into account that the internal resistance is *r = 3 Ohms*, we can write

$$I = \frac{(2/3)\varepsilon}{R_x + 3} = \frac{(2/3)\varepsilon}{R_x + r} = \frac{\varepsilon_1}{R_x + r},$$

In other words the circuit in Fig 4 is equivalent to the circuit in Fig. 5 where $\varepsilon_1 = (2/3)\varepsilon$

Then using this transformation 17 times we get the final result

$$I = \frac{(2/3)^{17}\varepsilon}{R_x + r} = \frac{(2/3)^{17}\cdot 10}{17 + 3} = 0{,}5\cdot(2/3)^{17} = 0{,}0005\ \mathrm{A}$$

**B**

**[3 *points*]** Light goes through the lens, reflects form the mirror and goes through the lens again. Therefore, putting a flat mirror next to the lens is equivalent to putting an identical lens next to the first lens. The distance of the object from the single lens and from the lens-mirror system is the same. The absolute magnification is the same as well. Since Γ = f/d, then absolute distance to the image is also the same(here f is the distance till the image, and d is the distance till the object). But the focal distance of the lens is twice as big as the focal distance of the lens-mirror system. It is easy to see that both images cannot be real at the same time or both virtual at the same time. Indeed, if both images are real, then

$$\Gamma_1 = \frac{F_1}{d - F_1};\qquad \Gamma_2 = \frac{F_2}{d - F_2}$$

So Γ₁ = Γ₂ implies F₁ = F₂. The same would hold if both images were virtual. We are left with the only alternative that one image is real and the other is virtual. Since F₁>F₂ = F₁/2, the image produced by a single lens is virtual, and the image produced by lens-mirror system is real. (For a virtual image d < F, and for a real image d > F.) Then

$$|\Gamma_1| = \frac{F}{F - d},\ |\Gamma_2| = \frac{F/2}{d - F/2}$$

Taking into account that |Γ₁ |= |Γ₂ | we get d = 2F/3, hence Γ = 3.

problems.title: Nuclear fusion
problems.statement:
One of the most important problems of modern plasma physics is the so-called controlled nuclear fusion. The most promising way of achieving the controlled nuclear fusion is the TOKAMAK, that is the magnetic trap for confining hot plasma.

The most perspective fusion reaction is based on hydrogen isotopes that are deuterium (D) and tritium (T) and it is symbolically written as

$$D + T \to {}^{4}He + n \qquad (1)$$

whereas the reaction products are the helium isotope ${}^{4}He$ and neutron $n$.

figures.caption: Fig.3. The cross section versus the relative energy of particles in the reaction expressed in $\mathrm{keV} = 10^3\mathrm{eV}$. $\sigma_0 = 10^{-28}\mathrm{m}^2$
figures.alt: Graph of σ/σ0 (vertical axis, 0 to 5) against E, keV (horizontal axis, 0 to 200) on a grid: the curve rises from about 0 near 10 keV to a maximum of about 5.1 near 65–70 keV, then decreases to about 1 at 200 keV.

parts.label: a)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** Assuming the particle masses are known, determine, analytically and numerically, the energy $E_0$, released in a single fusion reaction (1).

parts.label: b)
parts.statement: **[*0.5 points*]** In nuclear physics the energy is frequently counted in electron-volts (eV). One electron-volt is the energy that a single electron acquires passing an accelerating voltage of one volt. Calculate, analytically and numerically, the energy, found in question a), in electron-volts.

parts.label: c)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** Neglecting the initial energies of reacting particles, determine, analytically and numerically, the amounts of energy taken away by the helium nucleus $E_{He}$ and the neutron $E_n$.

answer.note: The printed formulas E_n = m_He/(m_He + m_n) and E_He = m_n/(m_He + m_n) omit the factor E0; the numbers correspond to the mass fractions times E0.

parts.label: d)
parts.statement: **[*1 point*]** In Tokamaks the deuterium-tritium mixture is heated up to a very high temperature, such that all the atoms are fully ionized (such a state is called a plasma) and their average kinetic energy is equal to $(3/2)k_BT$. To make reaction (1) possible it is necessary to overcome the Coulomb repulsion of reacting nuclei and bring them close to a distance of $a = 10^{-14}\mathrm{m}$ where nuclei attraction forces prevail. Estimate, analytically and numerically, the temperature $T$ at which reaction (1) becomes possible for the majority of the colliding particles.
parts.statementAfter: Fortunately, at thermal equilibrium the energies of particles are not even: some particles can have energy larger than $(3/2)k_BT$ while some might have less than $(3/2)k_BT$. Due to the presence of energetic particles the fusion reaction can take place even at temperatures lower than determined in d). The number of fusion reactions taking place per unit of time per unit of volume is given by the expression $n_Dn_T\sigma(\mathrm{v})\mathrm{v}$, where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the deuterium and tritium concentrations, respectively, $\sigma(\mathrm{v})$ is the so-called cross section of the reaction, and $\mathrm{v}$ refers to the relative velocity of the particles participating in the reaction.

parts.label: e)
parts.statement: **[*3 points*]** Determine, analytically and numerically, the average reaction rate $< \sigma(\mathrm{v})\mathrm{v} >$ at the temperature $T_0 = 10^8\mathrm{K}$, assuming that the effective velocity distribution is Maxwellian with the reduced mass $\mu = m_Dm_T/(m_D + m_T)$. The dependence of $\sigma(\mathrm{v})$ is graphically represented in the Fig.3 below.

parts.label: f)
parts.statement: **[*3 points*]** The matter heated to such a high temperature is in the state of plasma and the atoms are fully ionized. On the average, the total density of nuclei equals the density of electrons to satisfy the neutrality charge. To heat up the matter to the optimum temperature $T_0 = 10^8\mathrm{K}$ it is necessary to put in per unit of time a certain amount of energy, which should not exceed the amount released in fusion reactions. The energy of helium nucleus can totally be used for power production while only $\eta = 0.3$ of the neutron energy can be utilized. The rate of loss of thermal energy is given by $P_{loss} = E/\tau$, where $E$ is the energy density and $\tau$ is the time of plasma retention. Assuming that the particle concentrations are $n_D = n_T = n/2$, obtain, analytically and numerically, the inequality that guarantees the positive production of energy in a controlled nuclear fusion and relates the plasma concentration $n$ and retention time $\tau$.

parts.label: g)
parts.statement: **[*2.5 points*]** The plasma with temperature $T_0 = 10^8\mathrm{K}$ has a quite high pressure for a simple wall to sustain. A magnetic field, generated by a superconducting electromagnets of Tokamaks, is used to confine such matter. Magnetic field is used to compensate the thermal pressure. In the presence of magnetic field, the additional pressure due to magnetic field is $P = \gamma\mu_0^{\alpha}B^{\beta}$, where $\gamma = 1/2$, $\mu_0$ is the magnetic constant and $B$ is the magnetic field. Magnetic field is completely screened inside the plasma, so the additional pressure is absent there. Using dimensional analysis, find $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and determine, analytically and numerically, the magnetic field needed to confine the plasma with $n_D = n_T = n = 10^{20}\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

answer.note: α = −1, β = 2; the official solution prints the unit as „Ts“.

problems.statementAfterParts:
**Numerical values:**

Mass of deuterium $m_D = 3.34447\cdot 10^{-27}kg$,

Mass of tritium $m_T = 5.00732\cdot 10^{-27}kg$,

Mass of helium $m_{He} = 6.64432\cdot 10^{-27}kg$,

Mass of neutron $m_n = 1.67439\cdot 10^{-27}kg$,

Speed of light $c = 2.9979\cdot 10^{8}m/s$,

Elementary charge $e = 1.6022\cdot 10^{-19}C$,

Boltzmann constant $k_B = 1.3806\cdot 10^{-23}J/K$,

Electric constant $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854\cdot 10^{-12}\ F/m$,

Magnetic constant $\mu_0 = 1.257\cdot 10^{-6}\ H/m.$

***Note:***

The Maxwell distribution of the particle velocities with mass $\mu$ and temperature T has the following density function:

$$f(\mathrm{v}) = 4\pi\left(\frac{\mu}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2}\mathrm{v}^2\exp\left(-\frac{\mu\mathrm{v}^2}{2k_BT}\right)$$

solution.statement:
a) **[*1 point*]** In accordance with the Einstein formula the energy released in a single reaction is written as follows

$$E_0 = (m_D + m_T - m_{He} - m_n)c^2 = 2.973\cdot 10^{-12}\ J.$$

b) **[*0.5 points*]** The same energy is written in electron-volts as follows

$$E_0 = 2.973\cdot 10^{-12}/1.6022\cdot 10^{-19} = 1.856\cdot 10^{7}\ eV.$$

c) **[*1 point*]** If one can neglect the initial energies of reacting particles, the momentum and energy conservation laws immediately produce

$$E_n = \frac{m_{He}}{m_{He} + m_n} = 2.375\cdot 10^{-12}\ J = 1.482\cdot 10^{7}\ eV,$$

$$E_{He} = \frac{m_n}{m_{He} + m_n} = 5.984\cdot 10^{-13}J = 3.735\cdot 10^{6}\ eV.$$

d) **[*1 point*]** To overcome the Coulomb barrier nuclei should possess an appropriate thermal kinetic energy

$$\frac{3}{2}k_BT = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a}.$$

Thus

$$T = \frac{e^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0ak_B} = 1.115\cdot 10^{9}\mathrm{K}.$$

e) **[*3 points*]** The reaction rate is given by an average over the Maxwellian distribution as follows

$$< \sigma(\mathrm{v})\mathrm{v} > = \int_0^{\infty}\mathrm{v}\sigma(\mathrm{v})f(\mathrm{v})d\mathrm{v}$$

with the Maxwellian distribution function

$$f(\mathrm{v}) = 4\pi\left(\frac{\mu}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2}\mathrm{v}^2\exp\left(-\frac{\mu\mathrm{v}^2}{2k_BT}\right).$$

Introducing the dimensionless value $x = \mu\mathrm{v}^2/2k_BT$ and substituting the latter expression into the previous one can obtain

$$< \sigma(\mathrm{v})\mathrm{v} > = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sigma_0\sqrt{\frac{2k_BT}{\mu}}\int_0^{\infty}x\exp(-x)\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_0}\left(x\frac{k_BT_0}{e10^3}\right)dx = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sigma_0\sqrt{\frac{2k_BT}{\mu}}\int_0^{\infty}f(x)dx.$$

The integrand function $f(x)$ is drawn with the aid of the cross section figure as follows

Estimating the area under the line gives

$$< \sigma(\mathrm{v})\mathrm{v} > = 6.731\cdot 10^{-23}\frac{\mathrm{m}^3}{\mathrm{s}}.$$

f) **[*3 points*]** Plasma consists of electrons and ions and loses its thermal energy at time $\tau$. The effective power of losses in the unit of volume is given by the expression

$$P_{losses} = \frac{3nk_BT}{\tau}.$$

This power should be less than that produced in fusion reactions (see e)

$$P_{fusion} = \frac{n^2}{4}< \sigma(\mathrm{v})\mathrm{v} >\left(E_{He} + \eta E_n\right).$$

Thus, $P_{fusion} > P_{losses}$

$$n\tau > \frac{12k_BT_0}{(E_{He} + \eta E_n)< \sigma(\mathrm{v})\mathrm{v} >} \approx 1.982\cdot 10^{20}\frac{\mathrm{s}}{\mathrm{m}^3}.$$

This is the so-called Lawson’s criterion.

g) **[*2.5 points*]** Dimensional analysis immediately produces $\alpha = -1$ and $\beta = 2$. The thermal pressure of the plasma medium

$$P_{thermal} = 4nk_BT$$

should be compensated by the magnetic pressure from outside

$$P_{magnetic} = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.$$

Thus, $P_{thermal} = P_{magnetic}$

$$B = 2\sqrt{2\mu_0nk_BT_0} = 1.178\,\mathrm{Ts}.$$

figures.alt: Graph of the integrand f(x) (vertical axis, 0 to 0.12) against x (horizontal axis, 0 to 20): zero up to about x = 1, a sharp peak of about 0.125 near x ≈ 3.5, then decaying to nearly zero by x ≈ 11 and staying at zero to x = 20.
